title: Automotive Plastics & Glazing
subtitle: The Complete Guide to Interior, Exterior & Glazing Polymer Design
author: Subramanian J H

topics.title: Overview
concept: p

This book is about the plastics that make a car a place rather than a mechanism — the surfaces a driver touches, the faces a customer studies, the shields that take the stones, the lenses that carry the light, and the hundreds of small mechanisms that hold it all together. It is a companion to Body in White, and it shares that book’s conviction: that engineering is best taught not as a catalogue of parts but as a method — a disciplined way of asking questions that works on any surface, in any segment, on any vehicle.
p

The method rests on three questions, asked always in the same order. Is it functional? — does the part honour its duty across temperature, chemistry, load and appearance? Is it manufacturable? — can it be moulded, decorated and joined? Is it assemblable? — can it be married to the vehicle, serviced, and one day recovered? Everything in these pages — the material cards, the moulding physics, the design rules, the component chapters, the cases and the fleet transfer — is those three questions, asked of ever larger things.
p

The book is written from an Indian vantage: the summer soak of a black car in a Chennai car park, the monsoon that finds every undrained pocket, the ghat-road dust, the rupee that must be honestly spent, the respray culture that shapes exterior choices. But the method is universal, and the international engineer will find the physics unchanged under the local weather.
p

A word on the numbers. Throughout, the values given are representative and illustrative. This is deliberate: I would rather a young engineer learn to distrust a number and go and confirm it than memorise a figure that a grade change or a new regulation has quietly made wrong. No value in this book should be used as design data without verification against current datasheets, company standards and regulations.

topics.title: Overview
concept: p
The book is built in nine parts, and it can be read three ways.
p

Cover to cover, it builds an argument: Part I frames the cabin and its accounts; Part II chooses materials; Part III makes the part; Part IV supplies the method, rules, risk discipline, dimensional control and regulations; Part V walks the interior; Part VI the exterior; Part VII works three full cases; Part VIII carries the method across the fleet; Part IX into the electric future and back to the earth.
p

As a reference, it can be entered anywhere: each chapter is self-contained, opens with its role and the three questions, and closes with a standards snapshot, an FMEA-lite table and a set of questions a young engineer should be able to answer. The appendices gather the material, rules and dimension tables for the desk.
p

As a teacher, the two depth-template chapters — Chapter 20 (the instrument panel) for the interior and Chapter 26 (the bumper) for the exterior — are written at full reference depth, and in this Draft 2 every component chapter carries its master sections as their own titled sub-sections, each anchored to a dedicated dimensioned section drawing showing both neighbours. The pattern is constant: anatomy, construction by segment, master sections with neighbours and dimensions, regulations, assembly and BSR. Read the two demonstrators first, and the rest will read faster.
p

Two devices recur. The master section is a cut through an interface showing both neighbours, dimensioned, with the excursion arithmetic and the owning regulation in the margin — a treaty in ink. The five accounts (appearance, craftsmanship, safety, durability, BSR) are the currency in which every design decision is priced; a sixth, sustainability, joins them in the final chapter.
p
Cross-references are dense and deliberate — the book is a web, not a ladder. Follow them.
